steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) is used widely in smartphones, drones, vehicles and VR/AR devices. It measures linear velocity and angular rate continuously and tracks the motion of these platforms, as shown in Figure 1. Because of advances in Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) technology, MEMS IMUs today are small, energy-efficient and cost-effective. Inertial positioning (navigation) computes attitude, velocity and position from inertial measurements. This makes it important for many location-based applications, such as locating and navigating people in transportation infrastructures (e.g., airports, train stations), supporting security and safety services (e.g., helping first-responders), enabling smart city/infrastructure, and human-device interaction. Compared to other positioning solutions like vision or radio, inertial positioning is completely ego-centric, it works indoors and outdoors, and it is less affected by environmental factors such as complex lighting conditions and scene dynamics.

But the measurements from low-cost MEMS IMUs have several error sources, such as bias error, temperature-dependent error, random sensor noise and random-walk noise. In classical inertial navigation mechanisms the angular rates are integrated into orientation, and then based on that attitude the acceleration measurements are transformed into the navigation frame. Then the transformed accelerations are integrated twice into locations. Traditional inertial navigation algorithms are designed and described with concrete physical and mathematical rules. In ideal conditions the sensor errors are small enough that these hand-designed algorithms give accurate and reliable pose estimates. In real-world applications, however, the measurement errors cannot be avoided and they cause big problems for inertial positioning systems without constraints, which can fail within seconds. Even a minor error can be amplified exponentially in this process, and the result is unbounded error drift.

Previous researchers tried to deal with error drift in inertial navigation by adding domain-specific knowledge or other sensor. For pedestrian tracking it is important to use the periodicity of human walking. Pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) detects steps, estimates step length and heading, and updates the location of the user, which reduces the error drift from exponential to linear increase. Zero-velocity update (ZUPT) attaches the IMU to the foot of the user and detects the zero-velocity phase, and this is then used in Kalman filtering to correct the inertial navigation states. Drones or robots that have other sensors such as cameras or LiDAR can improve a lot over pure inertial solutions by integrating the inertial sensors with these modalities through filtering or smoothing. However these solutions are limited to specific application domains and they cannot solve the fundamental problem of inertial navigation.

Recently deep learning has shown impressive performance in many fields, including computer vision, robotics and signal processing. It has also been used for the challenges of inertial positioning. Deep neural network models have been used to calibrate inertial sensor noises, to reduce the drifts of inertial navigation mechanisms, and to fuse inertial data with information from other sensors. These works got a lot of attention because they show it is possible to use massive data to make data-driven models instead of relying on concrete physical or mathematical models. With the fast development of deep learning techniques, learning-based inertial solutions are becoming even more promising.

## I-A Taxonomy
- comprehensive review: measurement calibration, positioning algorithms, sensor fusion
- three levels (Figure 2)
  - sensor: calibration, model error sources, implicitly remove errors and noise
  - algorithm: replace modules of inertial navigation mechanisms, correct IMU integration; fusion with cameras, LiDAR -> accuracy, reliability
  - application: pedestrians, vehicles, drones, robots; learned motion patterns for PDR and ZUPT
- advantages / limitations; key challenges, future opportunities

## I-B Comparison with Other Surveys
- DL surveys: object detection, semantic segmentation, robotics; inertial positioning scarce
- broader ML-enhanced inertial sensing survey; ours narrower, past five years (2018-2022)
- pedestrian inertial positioning, indoor positioning, step length estimation, PDR surveys: no recent DL
- first thorough survey on the topic

## I-C Survey Organization
- II classical inertial navigation
- III, IV, V: calibration, navigation algorithms, sensor fusion
- VI-IX: pedestrian; vehicles, UAVs, robots; IMU-integrated positioning; human motion and activity recognition
- X: datasets, metrics, comparison
- XI: benefits, challenges, opportunities

However these solutions are limited to specific application domains and they cannot solve the fundamental problem of inertial navigation.

Recently deep learning has shown impressive performance in many fields, including computer vision, robotics and signal processing. It has also been used for the challenges of inertial positioning. Deep neural network models have been used to calibrate inertial sensor noises, to reduce the drifts of inertial navigation mechanisms, and to fuse inertial data with information from other sensors. These works got a lot of attention because they show it is possible to use massive data to make data-driven models instead of relying on concrete physical or mathematical models. With the fast development of deep learning techniques, learning-based inertial solutions are becoming even more promising.

## I-A Taxonomy

This survey wants to give a comprehensive review of deep-learning-based approaches to inertial positioning, including measurement calibration, inertial positioning algorithms and sensor fusion. To do this we set up a taxonomy of existing deep learning-based inertial positioning approaches, and we analyze how effective they are at three levels, the sensor level, the algorithm level and the application level, as shown in Figure 2.

- At the sensor level, deep learning is used as a calibration method for inertial sensors. It models the error sources in inertial measurements and removes corrupted measurement errors and noise implicitly.

- At the algorithm level, deep neural networks are built to partly or completely replace modules in traditional inertial navigation mechanisms, which enhances and corrects IMU integration in general. Deep learning is also a powerful tool for fusing inertial data with other sensor modalities such as cameras and LiDAR. These deep learning based IMU integration and fusion methods improve positioning accuracy and reliability.

- At the application level, we look at specific use cases where deep learning can be applied to inertial positioning for pedestrians, vehicles, drones and robots. For example we look at how learned motion patterns can improve pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) and zero-velocity update (ZUPT) algorithms.

Finally we discuss the advantages and limitations of the existing works in this domain, and we identify the key challenges and future opportunities in this research direction.

## I-B Comparison with Other Surveys

There are other deep learning surveys, for example on object detection, semantic segmentation and robotics, but surveys on deep learning based inertial positioning are relatively scarce and hard to find. There is a broader survey on machine learning enhanced inertial sensing, but our survey focuses more narrowly on deep learning based inertial positioning and gives deeper insights and analysis of the fast developments in this area in the past five years (2018-2022). Other relevant surveys, for example on inertial pedestrian positioning, indoor positioning, step length estimation and pedestrian dead reckoning, do not cover recent deep learning based solutions. As far as we know this article is the first survey that discusses deep learning based inertial positioning thoroughly and deeply.

## I-C Survey Organization

The rest of the survey is organized like this. Section II gives a short overview of classical inertial navigation mechanisms. Sections III, IV and V go into methods and algorithms for sensor calibration based on deep learning, inertial navigation algorithms and sensor fusion. Sections VI, VII, VIII and IX look at specific applications of deep learning in pedestrian inertial positioning, inertial positioning for vehicles, UAVs and robots, IMU-integrated positioning, and human motion and activity recognition. Section X presents representative public datasets, evaluation metrics and a performance comparison between learning-based and traditional inertial positioning models. Section XI concludes by discussing the benefits, challenges and opportunities.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) is widely used in smartphones, drones, vehicles, and VR/AR devices. It continuously measures linear velocity and angular rate and tracks the motion of these platforms, as illustrated in Figure 1. With advancements in Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) technology, today's MEMS IMUs are small, energy-efficient, and cost-effective. Inertial positioning (navigation) calculates attitude, velocity, and position from inertial measurements, which makes it a crucial element in various location-based applications, including locating and navigating individuals in transportation infrastructures (e.g., airports, train stations) [1], supporting security and safety services (e.g., aiding first-responders) [2], enabling smart city/infrastructure, and facilitating human-device interaction [3]. Compared to other positioning solutions such as vision or radio, inertial positioning is completely ego-centric, works both indoors and outdoors, and is less affected by environmental factors such as complex lighting conditions and scene dynamics.

Unfortunately, measurements from low-cost MEMS IMUs are subject to several error sources such as bias error, temperature-dependent error, random sensor noise, and random-walk noise. In classical inertial navigation mechanisms, angular rates are integrated into orientation, and acceleration measurements are transformed into the navigation frame based on the acquired attitude. The transformed accelerations are then doubly integrated into locations [4,5]. Traditional inertial navigation algorithms are designed and described using concrete physical and mathematical rules, and under ideal conditions sensor errors are small enough for these hand-designed algorithms to produce accurate and reliable pose estimates. In real-world applications, however, inevitable measurement errors cause significant problems for inertial positioning systems without constraints, which can fail within seconds, as even a minor error can be amplified exponentially, resulting in unbounded error drifts.

Previous researchers have tried to address error drifts in inertial navigation by incorporating domain-specific knowledge or other sensor. In pedestrian tracking, exploiting the periodicity of human walking is important: pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) detects steps, estimates step length and heading, and updates the user's location, mitigating error drifts from exponential to linear increase [6]. Zero-velocity update (ZUPT) attaches the IMU to the user's foot and detects the zero-velocity phase, which is then used in Kalman filtering to correct inertial navigation states [7]. Platforms such as drones or robots equipped with other sensors such as cameras or LiDAR can significantly improve on pure inertial solutions by integrating inertial sensors with these modalities through filtering or smoothing [8,9,10]. However, these solutions are limited to specific application domains and cannot address the fundamental problem of inertial navigation.

Recently, deep learning has shown impressive performance in various fields, including computer vision, robotics, and signal processing [11], and it has also been introduced to address the challenges of inertial positioning. Deep neural network models have been used to calibrate inertial sensor noises, reduce the drifts of inertial navigation mechanisms, and fuse inertial data with other sensor information. These works have attracted significant attention, as they show the potential of exploiting massive data to generate data-driven models instead of relying on concrete physical or mathematical models. With the rapid development of deep learning techniques, learning-based inertial solutions have become even more promising.

## I-A Taxonomy

This survey aims to provide a comprehensive review of deep-learning-based approaches to inertial positioning, including measurement calibration, inertial positioning algorithms, and sensor fusion. To this end, we establish a taxonomy of existing deep learning-based inertial positioning approaches and analyze their effectiveness at three levels: sensor level, algorithm level, and application level, as illustrated in Figure 2.

- At the sensor level, deep learning is employed as a calibration method for inertial sensors, effectively modeling error sources in inertial measurements and implicitly eliminating corrupted measurement errors and noise.

- At the algorithm level, deep neural networks are constructed to partially or completely replace modules in traditional inertial navigation mechanisms, enhancing and correcting IMU integration in general. Deep learning also serves as a powerful tool for fusing inertial data with other sensor modalities such as cameras and LiDAR. Such deep learning based IMU integration and fusion methods improve positioning accuracy and reliability.

- At the application level, we examine specific use cases where deep learning methods can be applied to inertial positioning for pedestrians, vehicles, drones, and robots, for instance how learned motion patterns can enhance pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) and zero-velocity update (ZUPT) algorithms.

Finally, we discuss the advantages and limitations of existing works in this domain, and identify the key challenges and future opportunities in this research direction.

## I-B Comparison with Other Surveys

Compared with other deep learning surveys, such as those on object detection [12], semantic segmentation [13], and robotics [14], surveys on deep learning based inertial positioning are relatively scarce and hard to find. While a broader survey on machine learning enhanced inertial sensing exists [15], our survey narrows the focus to deep learning based inertial positioning, providing deeper insights and analysis of the fast-evolving developments in this area over the past five years (2018-2022). Other relevant surveys, such as those on inertial pedestrian positioning [6], indoor positioning [16], step length estimation [17], and pedestrian dead reckoning [18], do not cover recent deep learning based solutions. To the best of our knowledge, this article is the first survey to discuss deep learning based inertial positioning thoroughly and deeply.

## I-C Survey Organization

The rest of this survey is organized as follows. Section II gives a brief overview of classical inertial navigation mechanisms. Sections III, IV, and V cover methods and algorithms for deep learning based sensor calibration, inertial navigation algorithms, and sensor fusion, respectively. Sections VI, VII, VIII, and IX explore specific applications of deep learning in pedestrian inertial positioning, inertial positioning for vehicles, UAVs, and robots, IMU-integrated positioning, and human motion and activity recognition, respectively. Section X presents representative public datasets, evaluation metrics, and a performance comparison between learning-based and traditional inertial positioning models. Finally, Section XI concludes by discussing the benefits, challenges, and opportunities.
